props.title: Planes, Trains and Automobiles
props.initialSlug: Two opposites endure chaotic journey home for Turkey Day

sections.content: Planes, Trains and Automobiles stands as John Hughes' masterpiece of adult comedy, perfectly pairing Steve Martin's uptight marketing executive Neal Page with John Candy's loveable but exasperating shower curtain ring salesman Del Griffith. The film elevates the road trip comedy genre by infusing genuine heart and pathos into what could have been a simple odd-couple narrative. Hughes, fresh off teen classics like The Breakfast Club (1985) and Ferris Bueller's Day Off (1986), brought his signature emotional depth to this Thanksgiving story, creating moments that shift seamlessly from hilarious chaos to touching humanity.

sections.content: The film's influence on road trip comedies cannot be overstated. Its DNA is evident in everything from Dutch (1991) to Little Miss Sunshine (2006). The "those aren't pillows" scene and the rental car meltdown have become comedy touchstones, but it's the quiet moments between Martin and Candy that elevate the film. Hughes shoots their nighttime hotel conversations with the same care he gave to the emotional cores of his teen films, allowing both actors to bring surprising depth to what could have been one-dimensional characters.

What sets the film apart is its masterful control of tone. While other comedies of the era like Trading Places (1983) or Stripes (1981) leaned heavily on their stars' comedic personas, Hughes forces both Martin and Candy to stretch dramatically. The revelation of Del's true circumstances in the film's final act transforms everything that came before, requiring a second viewing to fully appreciate the layers in Candy's performance. It's a technique that influenced later dramatic comedies like The Weather Man (2005) and Cedar Rapids (2011). SUBHEAD: The Hughes Touch

movies.title: Rain Man
movies.slug: Another masterful road movie that balances comedy and drama through mismatched traveling companions

sections.content: John Hughes brought his signature Americana sensibility to the film, painting a portrait of middle America that feels both satirical and loving. The various modes of transportation become characters themselves, from the hostile rental car agent to the chirpy bus driver, creating a tapestry of American travel that resonates with anyone who's ever faced holiday transportation chaos. This attention to environmental detail would influence later films like Away We Go (2009) and Up in the Air (2009).
